runs.u: Water boils at 100 degrees everywhere, right? My daughter's homework says altitude changes it and I told her that's wrong.
runs.reply: Actually, your daughter's homework is correct. Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level, but as you go higher in altitude, the air pressure decreases, and water boils at a lower temperature. So, at high elevations, water boils at a temperature lower than 100 degrees Celsius.

Why don't you tell her that you looked it up and it turns out she was right? You can say something like, 'Hey, I checked and it looks like your teacher was correct, water does boil at a lower temperature at high altitudes.' runs.u: Water boils at 100 degrees everywhere, right? My daughter's homework says altitude changes it and I told her that's wrong.
runs.reply: Actually, that's not entirely correct. Water does boil at 100 degrees Celsius (or 212 degrees Fahrenheit) at sea level, but its boiling point does decrease as altitude increases. This is because atmospheric pressure decreases with altitude, and water boils when its vapor pressure equals the surrounding pressure. So, at higher elevations, water boils at a lower temperature. Your daughter's homework is actually right!
